sets.title: The balcony table
sets.transcript:

M: I'm sorry, it gets really cold out there after six. The table by the big window has the same view, and it's warm.
W: Oh, okay. We'll take that one, then.

sets.title: The old bus depot
sets.transcript:
W: Oh, good, you're early. Can you help me put these chairs in a circle before the others get here?
M: Sure. Did you see the sign outside the old Kandel bus depot? They're knocking it down in March.
W: I did. That's what I want to bring up today. I think the club should write to the town council and ask them to keep the front of the building, at least the big arch over the gate.
M: I don't know. The council already voted on it, back in January. And my mom says the land's been sold to a builder.
W: Still, councils change their minds sometimes. If a whole school club writes, it's harder to ignore.
M: Maybe. But I'd rather do something we know will happen. My grandpa worked at that depot for almost thirty years. He fixed the buses. What if we filmed him walking around outside and talking about it?
W: Huh. Would he do that?
M: I think so. He tells those stories at every family dinner. Like, did you know the depot started out as a tram shed? He says the old rails are still under the concrete floor.
W: Seriously? So the building's older than the buses. That actually helps my letter. An old tram shed sounds a lot more worth saving than a bus garage.
M: Ha, maybe. But a letter takes weeks to get an answer, and by then it might be gone. A video we could finish in a weekend.
W: True, but a video doesn't save anything. It just remembers it.
M: Isn't that better than nothing?
W: Look, I don't want to decide this for everyone. Let's put both ideas to the club and let them vote.
M: Fair enough. Can I tell them about my grandpa first, before you talk about the letter?
W: Sure, go ahead. Oh, and you should check with him soon that he's really okay with being filmed.
M: I'll ask him when he picks me up after the meeting.

speakers.S: a teacher giving a short lecture to a high-school class

sets.title: Why Jastow moved uphill
sets.transcript:
OK, let's get started. Today I want to look at how the centre of a town can move over time, and I'm going to use one small example, the town of Jastow. You'll see this pattern in lots of places, but a small town makes it easier to follow.

Jastow began as a settlement beside a ford. A ford is a shallow place in a river where people and carts can cross. For roughly two hundred years, everything important in Jastow stood within a few minutes' walk of that crossing. The market square, the inn, the blacksmith and most of the houses were all right there.

Then things started to change. In eighteen sixty-four a stone bridge was built a little way upstream, and in eighteen eighty-five a railway station opened on the hill north of the town. By nineteen hundred, the busiest street in Jastow was the new high street running up to the station, and the old market square by the river was mostly warehouses.

So the obvious question is why. Why did a whole town centre climb a hill?

One explanation points to the railway. Goods and visitors now arrived at the top of the hill, so shops followed them. Think about it from a shopkeeper's point of view. You want to be where the people are. And there's good evidence for this. Business records show that three of the town's biggest stores moved up to the high street within ten years of the station opening.

But here's the interesting part. A second explanation points to the river itself. A set of old letters describes floods in the low streets in eighteen fifty-two and again in eighteen fifty-nine, years before the station existed. And a map drawn in eighteen seventy already shows new houses going up on higher ground. So some families may have been leaving the riverside before the trains came at all.

Now, which explanation is right? Honestly, we don't know yet, and both have weak spots. Let's start with the floods. All of those letters were written by members of one family, so we can't tell whether the water reached the whole lower town or just their street. And the new houses on the map might simply show Jastow growing, not people escaping the river.

The railway story has a problem too. Jastow's market licence, that's the document that gave the town the right to hold a weekly market, wasn't moved to the high street until nineteen ten. That's twenty-five years after the station opened. If the railway pulled everything uphill, why did the market stay down by the river for so long?

So historians are still arguing about it. Right now a local group is going through old tax records, which list who lived at each address every ten years. Those might finally settle it, or they might just raise new questions.

For Thursday, please look at the two maps in your packet, one from eighteen fifty and one from nineteen hundred, and write down three changes you notice between them.
